# Mathematical notes on cote 68, scans 45–56

## What the pages do

**45, a fixed order.** For an automorphism $u$ of a commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra $A$, let $J$ be generated by the differences $u(x)-x$. The proposition puts three conditions together: differential order at most $n$, $J^{n+1}=0$, and the existence of an ideal $I$ with $I^{n+1}=0$ on whose quotient $u$ acts identically. It gives $(u-\mathrm{id})^{n+1}=0$ as a sufficient condition, with a question in the margin about necessity.

**45, exponential and corollary.** The exponent bound returns in the assertion that $\Theta\mapsto\exp\Theta$ identifies the indicated nilpotent derivations with automorphisms satisfying the bound on $u-\mathrm{id}$. The following corollary drops the fixed order and includes the existence of a nilpotent logarithm among four purportedly equivalent conditions.

**46, reduction and scalars.** The first corollary compares the preceding conditions with the identity on $A_{\mathrm{red}}$ when the nilradical is nilpotent. The stated order bound uses its nilpotence exponent. The next corollary compares $K$-linearity of a nilpotent derivation with $K$-linearity of its exponential.

**46, a congruence ideal.** The last corollary defines $L_K(A,I)$ by $\Theta(A)\subset I$ and $G_K(A,I)$ by $(u-\mathrm{id})(A)\subset I$. It asserts a nilpotence bound for every such derivation, sketches a stronger inclusion for its powers, and displays an exponential identification. See R46a below.

**48, a game and a play.** A configuration has a player to move and a set of possible successor configurations. The same data are written as a relation $\Sigma$. The sheet distinguishes an initial configuration and the terminal configurations, then writes a play of $n$ moves as a tuple subject to the successor condition. The word “gagnantes” is crossed out in the definition of the terminal set.

**48, circular games.** Every player must occur, and the next player along a legal move must be obtained by applying a single map $\rho$ to the present player. The note gives a sufficient condition for uniqueness of $\rho$. The last numbered condition requires $\rho$ to be a cyclic permutation.

**50, two-element sets.** The first lemma lists tests for a map between two-element sets to be a bijection. They include comparison with the involution that exchanges the elements. The second lemma describes when a map $P\times Q\to R$ factors as an isomorphism from $P\wedge Q$, using its restrictions at the two elements of $P$.

**50, orientation and Stokes maps.** The proposed data assign $\Omega(V)$ to a real vector space, identify $\Omega(0)$ with the sign pair, and give a Stokes map for a hyperplane with a chosen side. Bijectivity and the effect of the opposite side are recast using two-element sets and the wedge construction. A map of theories is a natural transformation compatible with the distinguished data.

**50 and 52, existence and uniqueness.** The theorem asserts existence and unique isomorphism. Induction on dimension is invoked for invertibility and uniqueness. To investigate existence the author uses the standard spaces, their linear groups, their sign characters and the stabiliser of a hyperplane. Scan 52 gives a block matrix and a boxed compatibility equation involving the lower-right entry $\lambda$ and the $(n-1)$-dimensional block. After a cancelled paragraph it writes the character as sign composed with determinant.

**54, composition and the product sign.** The flag $U\subset W\subset V$ places a composite of two Stokes maps alongside product orientations. Exchanging the factors introduces the displayed dimension-dependent sign. A flag of real spaces, two rows about St applied to a product and a calculation in ordered basis vectors examine the signs. A square and a hatched quadrant with a curved arrow sit below the calculation. The rightmost basis subscript reaches the paper edge.

**56, graded determinant modules.** The sheet starts from finite free modules and isomorphisms over a commutative ring $k$. It proposes a tensor functor $\Delta$ to a graded Picard category, with sum-to-tensor comparison, unit and rank-one normalisations. For two complements of $W_1$ it gives a commutative diagram. A bracketed final criterion says that an automorphism acting identically on $W_1$ and the quotient acts identically under $\Delta$.

**51, 53 and 55, a literary list.** Each typescript compares joining pairs of words with threading stones on a necklace. The list begins with “lumière et ombre” and ranges over ways of knowing, states and oppositions. The three leaves have their own cancellations and pen corrections. Their word “jeu” belongs to this passage.

## Questions and conjectures

- **45.** “nécessaire ?” stands beside the sufficient condition on $u-\mathrm{id}$. The words immediately before the question are uncertain.
- **50.** “Existence d'une théorie de l'orientation ?” appears in the proof. The earlier raised words following “Existence” may also ask about existence of $\varphi$.
- **54.** The added sign has exponent $q$ or “?”. If it is a question mark it records an undecided sign. This is a reading question, with low confidence.
- **51, 53 and 55.** The rhetorical “Quel sens a un collier, si ce n'est le plaisir de le faire ...” belongs to the literary passage. No mathematical conjecture is attached to it.

- **54, product of orientations, page-file line 23.** The frozen target is $\Omega(V\wedge V')$. A second possible reading is $\Omega(V\times V')$. The little sign between the two V's is much smaller than the wedge on the source side. Its right stroke is thickened and the meeting point is indistinct. This is a low-confidence reading question.
- **56, sum-to-tensor comparison, page-file line 18.** The last factor is transcribed $\Delta(V')$. In this occurrence the opening parenthesis and the first stroke of the letter almost join, which can give the outline of $\Delta(W')$. The V's in the left side and the primes over the map favour the frozen reading. This is a low-confidence reading question.

## Remarks of the model

- **R46a · Model · high confidence.** The hypothesis $\Theta(A)\subset I$ alone does not give the asserted nilpotence. Take $K=\mathbb Q$, $A=\mathbb Q[t]/(t^2)$, $I=(t)$ and $\Theta(t)=t$. Here $I^2=0$ and $\Theta^2(t)=t$. The derivation rule and these values were checked on the basis $1,t$. The objection rests on the clear main assertion in S46c.
- **R46b · Model · high confidence.** A sufficient additional hypothesis for the power bound is $\Theta(I)\subset I^2$, together with the stated $\Theta(A)\subset I$. The product rule then gives $\Theta(I^j)\subset I^{j+1}$ for $j\geq1$. This is a possible refinement of the claim, supplied here by the model.
- **R45 · Model · high confidence.** The same algebra distinguishes two conditions of the unbounded corollary S45c. For the automorphism $u(t)=2t$, the difference ideal is $(t)$, yet $(u-\mathrm{id})(t)=t$. Here $u-\mathrm{id}$ agrees with the derivation in R46a on the basis $1,t$, so $u$ has differential order at most one. An exponential of a nilpotent derivation has nilpotent difference from the identity, so this $u$ cannot have the representation in (iv). This example also gives a negative answer if the marginal question concerns necessity of the sufficient condition.
- **R45g · Model · high confidence for the computation.** In the same example $u$ sends the class of $t$ in $J/J^2$ to twice itself. The marginal assertion S45d fails if it refers to every automorphism satisfying (i)–(iii). The page leaves the scope of the marginal note open.
- **R48 · Model · high confidence.** Given at least one legal move from a configuration assigned to each player, the compatibility equation fixes the value of $\rho$ on that player. This accounts for the weaker uniqueness hypothesis in S48.
